title: Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme (CPRS Fuel Credits) Bill 2009

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The speaker moved that the bills proceed without formalities, be taken together and read a first time, with a plan to later list them separately on the Notice Paper.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The speech announced the OzCar facility for car dealer financing, with a Commonwealth Guarantee covering around $550 million in securities, and introduced bills to strengthen journalists' privilege, streamline family tax benefit delivery, improve childcare administration and compliance, regulate life insurance non-operating holding companies, harmonise injunctions in prudential legislation, and amend fuel quality standards.

Senator Milne moved an amendment requiring the government to enter 2009 climate treaty negotiations with an unconditional commitment to reduce emissions by at least 25% below 1990 levels by 2020, and a willingness to reduce by 40% by 2020 under a global treaty.

speeches.speaker: Rachel Siewert
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Western Australia must diversify from the mining boom by investing in renewable energy and green jobs, criticised the government for spending $16 billion on clean coal instead, and called for a sustainable green economy with real emissions targets.

speeches.speaker: Nigel Scullion
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme is flawed, warning it will cost tens of thousands of jobs and harm investment without global participation. He criticised the government for rushing legislation before seeing international action, citing the failure of past unilateral fisheries policy as a parallel.

speeches.speaker: Scott Ludlam
speeches.brief: The Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme was opposed on grounds that it fails climate science targets (such as the 25–40% Bali range), subsidises polluters, and would increase global emissions by shifting industries overseas, citing figures like 20,000 jobs at risk in Wollongong and an $800 million cost to the cement industry; global warming science was also questioned, citing Lord Monckton and Dr Nils-Axel Morner, while Treasury modelling was criticised as inadequate and the delayed release of information was condemned.

Senator Milne moved an amendment requiring the government to enter climate treaty negotiations with an unconditional commitment to reduce emissions by at least 25% below 1990 levels by 2020, and a willingness to reduce by 40% by 2020 under a global treaty.

speeches.speaker: John Williams
speeches.brief: The senator argued that the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme would cause massive cost increases for businesses and households, citing Bayswater Power Station's coal costs rising from $350 million to $950 million annually and Bindaree Beef facing an extra $1 million per year in electricity bills, while offering negligible environmental benefit—reducing atmospheric CO₂ from 380 to 379 parts per million at a cost of $200 billion by 2020.

speeches.speaker: Dana Wortley
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme (CPRS) is essential for investing in renewable energies, creating low-pollution jobs, and positioning Australia as a leader in climate action, announcing a $75.8 billion Australian Carbon Trust, a $2.75 billion Climate Change Action Fund, a one-year delay to 2011, and a fixed carbon price of $10 per tonne. They urged passage of the bills to provide business certainty and avoid devastating climate impacts.

Senator Milne moved an amendment requiring the government to enter climate treaty negotiations with an unconditional commitment to reduce emissions by at least 25% below 1990 levels by 2020, and a willingness to reduce by 40% by 2020 under a global treaty.

speeches.speaker: Helen Kroger
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme should be delayed until after the Copenhagen climate talks and until the design of comparable schemes in the United States and other countries is known, warning it would destroy tens of thousands of jobs in industries like coal, aluminium, agriculture and manufacturing while having negligible impact on global emissions. The speaker cited a Frontier Economics report claiming an alternative scheme design could create 42,000 jobs in regional Australia instead of destroying 26,000, and noted that 45 per cent of voters wanted the scheme delayed until after Copenhagen.

speeches.speaker: Julian McGauran
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme bill is a massive new tax grab that will fund government expansion and patronage, not a climate solution. He said the legislation lacks critical detail on how it will affect agriculture and emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries, and urged slowing the process to allow technology to catch up.

Senator Milne moved an amendment requiring the government to enter 2009 climate treaty negotiations with an unconditional commitment to reduce emissions by at least 25% below 1990 levels by 2020, and a willingness to reduce by 40% under a global treaty.
